newsitem.title: USA: CSCE coffee rockets to new highs at close.
newsitem.headline: CSCE coffee rockets to new highs at close.

text.p: CSCE coffee futures soared to their highest level in two years on Monday, fueled by further news that supplies of coffee would remain tight for some time to come, industry sources said.
Traders said bullish statements by a U.S. Department of Agriculture official at an industry conference over the weekend touched off the market's initial rally.
USDA coffee analyst Edmond Missiaen said 1996/97 global output could come in lower than the 100.9 million bags the agency originally forecast last December.

"I would guess the next revision is more likely to be down than up," Missiaen told industry officials at the National Coffee Association's annual meeting in Scottsdale, Arizona, on Saturday. The USDA is not scheduled to publish another supply forecast until June 12.
Also underpinning sentiment on Monday was news dockworkers at Brazil's port of Paranagua are set to walk off the job for 24 hours on Wednesday.
While relatively little coffee is exported through Paranagua this time of year, traders said fears the strike would spread to other Brazilian ports heightened the market's already bullish tone.

In addition, traders pointed to a report from Merrill Lynch analyst Judith Ganes forecasting Colombia's 1996/97 crop to fall to 20-year lows. The crop would likely come in between 9.4 and 10.5 million 60-kg bags, Ganes said.

Finally, the market was aided by CFTC data showing a smaller-than-expected speculative long position. Commitment of Traders numbers released over the weekend showed speculators were net long some 14,000 lots as of February 25, including non-reportable positions.
"They weren't as long as people had thought, so that just opens room for more spec buying," said Albert Scalla, a trader with Hencorp Becstone in Miami.

Coffee prices have risen by more than 50 percent since the start of the year, as market participants reacted to steadily declining domestic stocks and signs of lower production in key countries like Colombia.

The most-active May contract rose by 8.00 cents a lb on the day, to 184.85 cents, the highest level on the weekly charts since March, 1995. The spot March contract, which expires in two weeks' time, rose 8.05 cents, at one point eclipsing the widely-watched 200.00 cent ($2) per lb mark.
"From a technical point of view, it's a very bullish market," Scalla said. "There is a marked lack of selling by origins...and some of the statements made by the USDA also helped."
Options were also active today, with out-of-the-money May and July calls well bid at 250.00 cents.
The day's volume reached an estimated 10,763 lots, compared with Friday's official total of 10,220.
((-- Wendy Pollack, New York Commodities Desk +1 212 859 1640))
